sections.b: Paul answers a question from the Corinthians about 'spiritual matters.' He says that gifts, services and workings are of many kinds but come from one Spirit, one Lord and one God, and that each is given 'for the good of all.' He lists nine gifts in 12:8-10 (a message of wisdom, a message of knowledge, faith, healings, works of power, prophecy, telling spirits apart, tongues, interpreting tongues) and eight in 12:28. His picture is the body, in which no part can say it does not need another, and the weaker parts get extra honor. The test of any gift is whether it builds up others.

sections.h: Love is greater than the gifts (1 Corinthians 13)
sections.b: Between his lists of gifts and his rules for using them, Paul puts a chapter on love. Tongues, prophecy, knowledge and faith without love are empty. Love lasts when prophecy and tongues have ended, and Paul says that the gifts are partial, 'for now.' Whether the end of the gifts is the return of Christ, or something earlier, is a question on which churches differ.

sections.h: Tongues and prophecy in the meeting (1 Corinthians 14)
sections.b: Paul ranks prophecy above tongues in the church's meeting because it can be understood and builds up everyone. Tongues are spoken 'to God' and need an interpreter. He rules that no more than two or three speak in tongues, in turn, that prophets speak in turn and are weighed by the others, and that everything be done in order. He ends by wishing that all spoke in tongues, but more that all prophesied, and by saying: do not stop anyone from speaking in tongues.

common: Paul's three chapters are about the church's meeting, and their central rule is that every gift must build up the church.
uncommon: The 'complete' of 13:10 is the finished New Testament, so tongues and prophecy ended when it was complete (a cessationist reading; most scholars read it as the return of Christ).

claude.title: Tongues last in both lists
claude.body: Paul places tongues last in both lists (12:10, 12:28) and ends the questions of 12:29-30 with them, a quiet way of lowering the gift the Corinthians prized most without denying that it is the Spirit's.

sections.h: The Spirit and the confession 'Jesus is Lord' (1 Corinthians 12:3, 13)
sections.b: Paul gives the Corinthians a test of the Spirit's presence that has nothing to do with unusual experience: no one who speaks by the Spirit of God says 'Jesus is under a curse,' and no one can say 'Jesus is Lord' except by the Holy Spirit. He then says that 'in one Spirit all of us were baptized into one body' and 'were given one Spirit to drink.' Churches differ on whether the verse refers to conversion, to water baptism, or to a second experience.

Paul says that all believers, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free, were baptized 'in one Spirit' into one body. The verse is used in teaching on both water baptism and baptism in the Spirit. It does not say whether the baptism is the rite or the Spirit's work, and the churches read it according to their teaching on baptism.

sections.h: Prophecy in the Corinthian church (1 Corinthians 12-14)
sections.b: New Testament prophecy was a spoken message in the meeting for 'building up, encouragement and comfort' (14:3). It was to be weighed by the others (14:29), and Paul calls it partial (13:9). Scholars differ on whether it carried the authority of the Old Testament prophets or was a more limited gift. The unbeliever who hears it is convicted and worships God (14:24-25).

Paul lists 'the same Spirit,' 'the same Lord' and 'the same God' as the source of the gifts, services and workings. The verses do not teach the doctrine of the Trinity, but they are among the New Testament pattern of Father, Son and Spirit acting together that later churches used when they spoke of three who are one.

Paul names 'gifts of healings' (both words plural) among the Spirit's gifts and asks in 12:30 whether all have them. He expects the answer 'No.' The gift is a gift of the community, given as the Spirit decides, not a standing office held by one person.

Paul's list of what God has placed in the church begins with apostles, then prophets and teachers. The order is numbered, 'first, second, third,' and the rest follow with 'then.' Apostles are first as founders (3:10); Ephesians 2:20 says the church is built on the apostles and prophets.

sections.h: 'The women are to be silent' (1 Corinthians 14:34-35)
sections.b: One of the passages that limits women's roles, and one of the most debated. Paul seems to assume in 11:5 that women pray and prophesy aloud in the meeting; in 14:34-35 women are told to be silent and to ask their husbands at home. Readings: a general ban; a ban on one kind of speech, such as weighing prophecy or asking questions; a rule against disorder; a rule for married women; a local and temporary rule; a quotation Paul rejects; a later addition to the letter. Some manuscripts place the verses after verse 40.

sections.h: Worship that everyone can follow (1 Corinthians 14)
sections.b: Paul asks that the church's meeting be understood by all, including outsiders: a person who cannot follow a prayer cannot say 'Amen' to it (14:16), and a visitor who hears nothing but tongues will think the church is mad (14:23). His list of what the Corinthians bring to a meeting (a psalm, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, an interpretation) is one of the few pictures of early Christian worship. He ends with 'let everything be done in a proper way, with order.'

Paul's instructions on the gifts show what a meeting in Corinth looked like: a house gathering of a few dozen with many voices, a mix of Jews and former pagans, with outsiders and visitors who could walk in. The church's pride in its spiritual experience was a problem of rank, and Paul's answer is the picture of one body in which the weak get extra honor.

Paul writes of speaking 'the languages of humans and of angels.' Jewish writings of the time describe angels with their own languages: in the Testament of Job, Job's daughters speak in the dialect of the angels. Paul may be using exaggeration, or answering a Corinthian claim.

Paul reminds his Gentile readers of their former worship and uses the Old Testament's mockery of idols as mouths that cannot speak (Psalm 115:5; Habakkuk 2:18) as a contrast with the Spirit who gives speech. He warns that powerful religious experience, such as they knew in the cults, does not prove which spirit is at work.

Paul says we see now through a mirror, in a riddle, 'but then face to face,' and that we will know fully as we are known. The phrases recall what God says of Moses, who saw the form of the LORD 'openly and not in riddles' (Numbers 12:8), and Exodus 33:11 and Deuteronomy 34:10 on speaking 'face to face.'

Paul uses musical pictures twice: speech without love is 'ringing bronze, a clashing cymbal' (13:1), and a flute, a lyre or a trumpet must give distinct notes to be understood (14:7-8). He also speaks of singing 'with the spirit' and 'with the mind' (14:15) and lists 'a psalm' among what the Corinthians bring to the meeting (14:26).

sections.h: Praying with the spirit and the mind (1 Corinthians 14:14-15)
sections.b: Paul says that if he prays in a tongue, 'my spirit prays, but my mind produces nothing.' His answer is to pray with both: 'with my spirit, and with my mind as well.' The same is true for singing. Churches differ on whether praying in tongues in private is a gift to seek; Paul says he speaks in tongues more than any of them (14:18).

sections.h: 'If one part suffers, all suffer' (1 Corinthians 12:26)
sections.b: In the body picture Paul says the members share suffering and honor, 'rejoicing' with the one honored. The verse has been used for the unity of all believers, including the living and the dead, in the one body of Christ, a teaching held in different forms by Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant writers.

sections.h: 'Slaves or free' in one body (1 Corinthians 12:13)
sections.b: Paul lists Jews and Greeks, slaves and free people as all baptized into one body. The line does not end slavery, and Paul deals with it elsewhere (1 Corinthians 7:21-24), but it makes slave and free members of one body, with the same Spirit.
